name: Mituku
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 4 other works read were silent
catalog_citation: Goldsmith, John. 2002. Tone in Mituku: How a floating tone nailed down an intermediate level. In Jacques Durand & Bernard Laks (eds.), Phonetics, phonology, and cognition, 80-95. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Read from the author's open preprint 'Access to an intermediate level for tonal constraints: tone in Mituku' (30 pp., https://people.cs.uchicago.edu/~jagoldsm/Papers/mituku.pdf; PDF metadata 'Microsoft Word - ', 2007). Data source of the paper: Stappers, Leo. 1973. Esquisse de la langue mituku. Tervuren: MRAC, Annales Sciences humaines 80 (print only, not opened).
catalog_locator: Preprint §2 'Some basic facts about Mituku', pp. 4-5 of 30 (text layer); the only occurrences of 'stress'/'accent' are in §8 'A speculative note', pp. 23-24 (txt, 1015), general theory not applied to Mituku. Published chapter pp. 80-95 not opened.
catalog_quote: 1. On the surface, a syllable will bear one of four identifiable tones: High, Low, Falling, or Rising; in addition, between two Highs (or a High and a Falling tone), downstep (also known as tone slip) can occur. Downstep is well-known to students of tone languages; its phonetic manifestation is a lowering by about a whole step (in the ordinary musical sense of the term) of the pitch of a High tone, and all subsequent High tones in the phrase. We will see shortly that the downstep is the result of a floating Low tone, a state of affairs frequently found among African languages. It is not hard to show that the Falling tone is the result of the concatenation of a High tone and a Low tone, and that the Rising tone is the result of the concatenation of a Low tone and a High tone. ... there is no surface vowel length contrast (and there is no underlying vowel length contrast either, a separate matter), regardless of the source and composition of the surface vowel in question. This is the first of the two important facts about Mituku tone to bear in mind. The second important fact is this: a contour tone (i.e., Rising or Falling tone) may appear on a vowel if and only if that vowel is the realization of two underlying vowels (or vowel positions, to make the same point in slightly different terms).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (30 pp., PDF metadata 'Microsoft Word - Mituku3.doc', 2007, author John; title page 'Access to an intermediate level for tonal constraints: tone in Mituku', John Goldsmith, University of Chicago) and its text layer. Section '2 Some basic facts about Mituku' begins at the top of preprint p. 4 (the text layer). The quoted passage is there word for word: '1. On the surface, a syllable will bear one of four identifiable tones: High, Low, Falling, or Rising; in addition, between two Highs (or a High and a Falling tone), downstep (also known as tone slip) can occur.' (p. 4) and, after the elided sentences on downstep/floating Low and vowel hiatus, 'there is no surface vowel length contrast…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mituku is a tone language: every syllable surfaces with H, L, falling or rising tone, with downstep between Highs caused by a floating Low; verb radicals, subject markers, object markers and tense markers each carry lexical H or L (the analysis rejects a H/zero account); contour tones arise only where two underlying vowels merge; there is no vowel-length contrast. No accessible source says anything about word stress or accent in Mituku.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress; the paper's exceptions concern where the floating Low docks (historic past vs optative tense markers, Meeussen's rule, rising-tone absorption).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level verbal tonology (infinitives and finite verb forms) analysed from Stappers 1973's data, not from the author's own fieldwork; the tone facts are Stappers', the analysis is Goldsmith's.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Mituku of the Ponthierville (Ubundu) area between the Lomami and Lualaba (mitu1240; self-name kinyamituku, older keleka). The 1970 texts come from a single informant, Isidore Agbamubi of the village Biimbi. Salumbu 1978 covers the Kesikate dialect under the name Metoko; no separate glottocode exists for it.

sources.locator: §2 'Some basic facts about Mituku', preprint pp. 4-5 (published chapter pp. 80-95)
sources.note: Whole paper is a tonal analysis built on Stappers 1973: four surface tones (H, L, falling, rising) plus downstep from a floating L; H/L lexical contrast in every verbal morpheme class; no surface or underlying vowel-length contrast. The words 'stress'/'accent' occur only in general theoretical remarks (metrical grids, accent systems), never applied to Mituku; no word-stress statement.
